You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis
The test `testDontQuoteEuroFirstChar` expects that when printing a CSV record where the first character is the Euro sign (€), the output should not quote the Euro character, and the CSV should be output as `€` followed by the other value and the record separator, i.e. `€,Deux\r\n`.

The current bug report describes a related problem regarding quoting behavior when the first string contains CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) characters: Apache Commons CSV outputs the first CJK field as quoted `"あ"`, whereas Microsoft Excel outputs it unquoted `あ`.

Looking at the relevant source code sections:

- The `CSVPrinter.printRecord(Object...)` method delegates to the CSVFormat's `printRecord(Appendable, Object...)`.

- `CSVFormat.printRecord` calls `print(Object value, Appendable out, boolean newRecord)` for each value. The `newRecord` boolean indicates if the value is the first in the record.

- `CSVFormat.print(Object value, Appendable out, boolean newRecord)` calls `printAndQuote` if a quote character is set.

- `printAndQuote` performs the quoting decision based on QuoteMode. In the `MINIMAL` mode (the default in many cases including Excel), there is special logic for values at the start of a record (`newRecord == true`). Quoting is enforced if the first character `c` meets certain criteria:
  - It is less than 0x20 (control characters)
  - or between 0x21 and 0x23 etc. (a range of ASCII characters)
  - or greater than 0x7E (non-ASCII)

In particular, the condition on line 1189 states:
```java
if (newRecord && (c < 0x20 || c > 0x21 && c < 0x23 || c > 0x2B && c < 0x2D || c > 0x7E)) {
    quote = true;
}
```

This complex condition includes `c > 0x7E` which covers non-ASCII characters, including Euro sign and CJK characters.

Thus, for the first character in a new record that is Euro or CJK, quoting will be enforced by Apache Commons CSV whereas Excel does not quote them.

This difference leads to the failures:
- The test `testDontQuoteEuroFirstChar` expects no quoting for Euro first char, but it gets quoted due to the above condition.
- The current bug report observes quoting for the first CJK character that Excel doesn't do.

In summary, the bug is caused by the quoting condition in `printAndQuote` method that enforces quoting on first characters above ASCII 0x7E, which differs from Excel's behavior of not quoting Euro or CJK characters at the start of a record.

The current implementation's quoting logic for first characters is too aggressive in quoting Unicode characters > 0x7E, resulting in non-Excel-compatible CSV output regarding quotes.

This diagnosis aligns with the test failure and the bug report's description of the quoting behavior discrepancy for CJK chars and Euro first char.

No recent bug reports appear relevant to this quoting logic issue.

This suggests the fix should address the quoting condition in the `printAndQuote` method, specifically handling first character quoting for Unicode characters to better match Excel behavior.

Recommended focus is on the part of the condition in `printAndQuote` that decides quoting for `newRecord` when the first char is Euro or CJK.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).

org.apache.commons.csv.CSVFormat.print(Object, Appendable, boolean)
org.apache.commons.csv.CSVFormat.printAndQuote(Object, CharSequence, int, int, Appendable, boolean)
